Your fork may be too soft overall: it can dive into the firm part of its travel, feel harsh there, then bottom on landings.

First, check the fork air pressure cold with the front wheel off the ground and bleed the fork; GasGas’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Record your current clicker position before changing it.

- If it dives and rides deep, turn fork compression **1 click in** from where it is now for more support.
- If it instead rides high and deflects sharply on the chop, try **1 click out** from your current compression setting for compliance.

Test the same section for a few laps and return to your starting setting if it gets worse. If the chop improves but it still bottoms hard, pressure or fork service may need attention rather than more clicks.

Does the front dive and ride low, or sit high and bounce off the chop?

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork compression — if diving and riding deep:** Turn 1 click in from the current setting.
- **Fork compression — alternative if riding high and deflecting:** Turn 1 click out from the current setting.

The likely cause is **shock damping fading as it heats up**. Oil gets thinner when hot; worn internals, aerated oil or lost nitrogen pressure can make the rebound control fall away further.

With the bike off and the shock cool, check the shock shaft, body and reservoir for oil leakage or damage. A dry shock can still have an internal fault. If the rear ride height also drops after riding, Honda says to check the damper for nitrogen loss.

**Stop riding until it’s checked** if the rear is bouncing enough to affect control. Don’t open the pressurized shock; a suspension shop can test and service it. How many hours are on the shock since its last service?
The heat-related bouncing points to shock damping fade, not a clicker setting to chase.

Yes. The tire is the first part of the suspension to hit a bump: **higher pressure** feels firmer and can deflect off sharp edges; **lower pressure** adds compliance and grip, but too little lets the tire squirm and risks pinch flats or rim damage.

Honda’s cold baseline for your CRF450R is **15 psi (100 kPa) front and rear**. Check it cold before changing clickers. For slick ground, try 1 psi lower; for rocks or hard landings, try 1 psi higher. Test the same section and stop going lower if the tire squirms or the rim strikes.

With **105 mm rider sag but only 20 mm static sag**, the shock spring is likely too soft for you. It takes enough preload to leave the rear sitting high when you get off. GasGas’s targets are **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**.

First, remeasure both with the bike upright and check that the linkage moves freely. If the readings repeat, go one spring rate stiffer rather than adding more preload. For example, **if a 42 N/mm shock spring is fitted**, 45 N/mm is a reasonable first step; reset rider sag and confirm static sag afterward. Don’t chase this with clickers.

On your CRF450R’s **standard 56 N/mm shock spring**, don’t shorten the installed spring length below **222.9 mm (8.78 in)**. Honda’s permitted range is 222.9–233 mm; its standard setting is 232.3 mm (9.15 in).

Measure the spring seat-to-seat with the rear wheel off the ground. One adjuster turn changes its length by 1.5 mm. Set preload to reach **105 mm race sag**, measured with you seated in full gear. If you need to go below the minimum length to reach sag, the spring is too soft—fit a stiffer one rather than forcing more preload.

Honda doesn’t publish a free-sag target for this bike. As general guidance, around 25–35 mm is a useful check: with race sag set, very little free sag also points toward a spring that’s too soft.
On the standard shock spring, less than 222.9 mm installed length is too much preload.

First, **repeat the race-sag measurement the same way** before changing preload. Differences in rider position, gear or fuel can change the reading; a binding linkage or a loose preload adjuster can also make it vary.

For your CRF250R, Honda measures from the center of the left rear-fender bolt to the center of the chain-adjuster locknut. Subtract the rider-aboard measurement from the measurement with the rear wheel off the ground. With the standard shock spring, the target is **105 mm**, measured at race weight with fuel to the bottom of the filler neck.

Have a helper measure with you in full gear and the same riding position each time. Gently settle the rear before each reading. Also look for a loose preload locknut, shock oil or linkage play; friction is more likely if the rear settles at different heights when pushed down versus lifted up.

How many mm is your rider sag changing between rides? If the adjuster is loose, the shock is leaking or the linkage has play, fix that before riding.
Changing sag can come from an inconsistent measurement, suspension friction or a moving preload adjuster. Repeat the measurement before adjusting it.

Release the built-up air **after practice and between motos**, with the fork fully extended and the front wheel off the ground.

1. Let the forks cool, then put the bike securely on a stand.
2. Clean around the small air-release screw on each fork cap. Loosen each screw to let the pressure escape, then refit it. Don’t turn the compression adjuster by mistake.
3. Check the screw O-rings and tighten the screws carefully. The release-screw torque for your US bike isn’t confirmed here; check the fork section of Honda’s competition handbook for that value.

I can walk you through **Release built-up air from the fork** in the app—tap “Working on the bike?” above the message box.

Your MC 250F has a **WP XACT AER air fork**. For routine care, bleed the outer chambers with the fork cold, engine off and front wheel off the ground: loosen the bleeder screw on each fork cap, let the air out, then tighten both screws. These bleeders are **not** the main spring-air valve.

For a full air-side service:
1. Release the main spring pressure through its air valve before attempting to remove the air-spring assembly. Don’t rely on the outer-chamber bleeders to depressurize it.
2. The complete internal teardown and reassembly procedure isn’t confirmed here; use the correct WP service procedure or have a suspension shop do that portion. Internal chambers can remain hazardous if handled incorrectly.
3. For the stock fork, GasGas lists **5 g of special grease for the left cartridge** and **230 ml of SAE 4 fork oil in each outer mechanism**. That outer oil is separate from the air cartridge; don’t substitute the right damping cartridge’s oil quantity.
4. After assembly, set the main spring pressure cold to the stock reference of **10.4 bar (151 psi)** and check for leaks.

GasGas calls for fork service once after **10 hours**, then every **40 hours**; harsh conditions can shorten that interval.

I can walk you through the separate “Release built-up air from the fork and clean the dust boots” job. Tap **Working on the bike?** above the message box; have a lift stand, bleeder screwdriver, clean rags and universal oil spray ready. Keep oil off the brake disc; if oil is dripping from a boot, have the seal checked before riding.

Yes. New seals and bushings can feel sticky at first, so start with an easy ride and let the suspension work through its travel before judging harshness or changing clickers. A rebuild with few replacement parts may change feel less. Honda doesn’t specify a suspension break-in duration here.

Afterward, check for leaks, recheck race sag—Honda’s target with the standard shock spring is **105 mm**—and release fork air with the front wheel off the ground and forks fully extended. Tighten each fork plug bolt to **1.3 N·m (1.0 ft-lb)**. Once the feel is consistent, tune one click at a time.

For a **new bike**, Honda calls for replacing the fork oil after the first break-in ride; that instruction doesn’t by itself establish an oil change after every fork rebuild.

A **leak-down test** feeds regulated air into the cylinder with the piston at top dead center on the compression stroke. The gauge shows the percentage of air leaking out, and listening tells you where it’s going:

- **Intake:** air at the throttle body points toward an intake valve.
- **Exhaust:** air at the tailpipe points toward an exhaust valve.

- **Cooling system:** bubbles can indicate a head-gasket or head sealing problem.

A compression test instead measures the pressure the engine builds while cranking. It’s a useful overall check, but it doesn’t pinpoint the leak; cranking speed and decompression hardware can also affect the reading.

**Squish clearance** is the gap between the piston crown and the outer band of the cylinder head when the piston is at the top of its travel.

As the piston rises, that band squeezes the fuel-air mixture toward the spark plug. Builders set the clearance to promote a faster, more consistent burn and reduce the tendency to detonate. Squish is the clearance between the piston and cylinder head at the edge of the chamber. Builders set it to control combustion without letting the piston touch the head.
